solutions.latex: $\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{10} f(x)\,dx$ gives the value of the definite integral from $x=-5$ to $x=10$. The region from $x=4$ to $x=10$ is negative, so $\left|\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{10} f(x)\,dx\right|$ does not give the area.

False statement: "$X$ and $Y$ are independent events".

$P(Y\mid X)=\dfrac{P(Y\cap X)}{P(X)}$, so $\dfrac{P(Y\cap X)}{0.5}=0.7$ and $P(Y\cap X)=0.35$.

$P(Y)\times P(X)=0.5\times 0.6=0.3\neq 0.35$, so not independent.

Option A is the definition of the derivative.

Option B: the expression represents the gradient of the line joining $A\left(x-\dfrac{h}{2},f\left(x-\dfrac{h}{2}\right)\right)$ and $B\left(x+\dfrac{h}{2},f\left(x+\dfrac{h}{2}\right)\right)$. As $h\to 0$, this will give the gradient of the tangent at $(x,f(x))$.

Option C: the expression represents the gradient of the line joining $(x-h,f(x-h))$ and $(x,f(x))$. As $h\to 0$, this will give the gradient of the tangent at $(x,f(x))$.

Option D: the expression is equivalent to $-f'(x)$ (the opposite of Option C), which is not the same as $f'(x)$.

solutions.latex:
For a PDF $f(x)$ with domain $a\le x\le b$, the CDF is given by $P(X\le x)=F(x)=\displaystyle\int_a^x f(x)\,dx$.

$F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,dx=\left[-e^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^x=-e^{-\lambda x}+1=1-e^{-\lambda x}$

Or more formally: $F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<0\\ 1-e^{-\lambda x} & x\ge 0\end{cases}$

solutions.latex:
$\sin x-\sin x\tan x-1+\tan x=0$

$\sin x(1-\tan x)-(1-\tan x)=0$

$(\sin x-1)(1-\tan x)=0$

$\sin x=1$ or $\tan x=1$

For $\sin x=1\Rightarrow x=\dfrac\pi2$, but this does not satisfy the original equation, because $\tan\dfrac\pi2$ is undefined.

$\therefore\tan x=1\Rightarrow x=\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac{5\pi}4$

Marker's comment: Most students found this difficult. Dividing both sides by $(1-\tan x)$ assumes $1-\tan x\neq 0$; instead bring all terms to the LHS, factorise and use the Null Factor Law. Check solutions by substituting back, as $x=\pi/2$ does not satisfy the original equation because $\tan\pi/2$ is undefined.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: 1 mark for factorising (taking out $\sin x$ as a common factor, or equivalent); 2 marks for finding $\frac\pi2$ and then ruling it out; 2 marks for three solutions $\frac\pi4,\frac{5\pi}4,\frac\pi2$ (as printed in the guideline)

$S=14+18+\dots$, $a=14$, $d=4$

$S_n=\dfrac n2[2a+(n-1)d]=\dfrac n2[2(14)+4(n-1)]=\dfrac n2(24+4n)=12n+2n^2\le 1320$

$2n^2+12n-1320\le 0$, so $n^2+6n-660\le 0$

$n=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{6^2-4(1)(-660)}}{2(1)}$, $n=-28.8$ or $22.8$

$\therefore S_n\le 1320$ if $n\le 22.8$, so $n=22$ is the maximum number of rows.

solutions.latex:
Let $P$ be the point on the circle furthest from the origin.

\exfigure{730_q30_s1}

(Note: $O(0,0)$, $C(1,2)$ and $P$ must be collinear; if not, the direct distance $OP$ would be shorter than $OC+CP$.)

The equation of the diameter through the centre and $P$ is $y=2x$. Solve simultaneously with the circle:

$x^2-2x+(2x)^2-4(2x)=15$

$5x^2-10x=15$, so $x^2-2x-3=0$, $(x-3)(x+1)=0$, $x=3$ or $-1$.

When $x=3$, $y=6$, so $P=(3,6)$.

Alternative method:

\exfigure{730_q30_s2}

$OC=\sqrt{1^2+2^2}=\sqrt5$, $PC=2\sqrt5$ (radius).

$\tan\angle COA=\dfrac{AC}{OA}=\dfrac21$, so $\angle COA=\tan^{-1}2$ ($\approx 63.43^\circ$), hence $\angle PCB=\tan^{-1}2$ (corresponding angles on parallel lines).

$\sin\angle PCB=\dfrac{PB}{2\sqrt5}$, so $PB=2\sqrt5\sin(\tan^{-1}2)=4$; similarly $BC=2\sqrt5\cos(\tan^{-1}2)=2$.

$\therefore P=(1+2,2+4)=(3,6)$

solutions.latex:
$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=4\cos\theta(1+\cos\theta)-4\sin\theta\sin\theta=4\cos^2\theta-4\sin^2\theta+4\cos\theta$

$=4(\cos^2\theta-(1-\cos^2\theta)+\cos\theta)=4(2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1)=4(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)$

$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$ when $\cos\theta=-1,\dfrac12$, so $\theta=180^\circ,60^\circ$. As $\theta$ is acute, $\theta=60^\circ$.

Check it is a maximum:

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc}\theta&50^\circ&60^\circ&70^\circ\\ \hline \frac{dA}{d\theta}&0.719&0&-1.69\end{array}$$

$\therefore$ maximum area when $\theta=60^\circ$

solutions.latex:
$f'(x)=2\cos 2x-1$, so $f'\left(\dfrac\pi4\right)=2\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2\right)-1=-1$

$f\left(\dfrac\pi4\right)=\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2\right)-\dfrac\pi4=1-\dfrac\pi4$

Tangent: $y-\left(1-\dfrac\pi4\right)=-\left(x-\dfrac\pi4\right)$, so $y=1-x$.

Points of intersection: $1-x=\sin 2x-x$, $\sin 2x=1$, $2x=\dfrac\pi2$ or $-\dfrac{3\pi}2$, $x=\dfrac\pi4$ or $-\dfrac{3\pi}4$.

$A=\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{3\pi}4}^{\frac\pi4}(1-x)-(\sin 2x-x)\,dx=\int_{-\frac{3\pi}4}^{\frac\pi4}(1-\sin 2x)\,dx=\left[x+\dfrac12\cos 2x\right]_{-\frac{3\pi}4}^{\frac\pi4}$

$=\left(\dfrac\pi4-\dfrac12\cos\dfrac\pi2\right)-\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}4-\dfrac12\cos\dfrac{3\pi}2\right)=\dfrac\pi4+\dfrac{3\pi}4=\pi$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 5: correct solution; 4: correct progress up to correct antiderivative for area with endpoints; 3: up to correct x coordinate of point A; 2: up to correct equation of the tangent; 1: up to correct gradient of the tangent
